For years I believed the only way to lose weight was to give up roti, rice, sweets, and everything that felt like home.

Then I did something that felt almost wrong at first:

I started eating more of the foods I loved—roti, dal, rice, thepla, paneer, sweets—yet I lost the weight and got my energy back.

I made sure every meal had enough protein—80–100 g a day from dal, paneer, soya, curd, doodh. (I used to eat only 40–50 g without realising.)

I finished dinner by 8 pm latest (most days 7:30 pm). No late-night khichdi or paratha. Just protein + vegetables + a little ghee.

I walked 8,000–10,000 steps every day—nothing fancy, just walking after dinner or during calls.

I drank one glass of warm haldi doodh every night with a pinch of jaiphal. That small habit alone changed my sleep and my cravings.
That’s it.

No expensive supplements, no keto, no starving.

Just normal veg home food, timed differently and with more protein than before.

Today I’m back to my college weight, my TSH is 1.9 (never started thyroid medicine), and I wear saree again without hiding anything.
I still eat sweets sometimes, and I still eat roti every day.

My father is 69. Three diagnoses, seven pills… and still tells me ‘I’m fine, don’t overthink.’”

 Retired. Two children doing well in their careers, life seemingly sorted from the outside.

High blood pressure.
Type-2 diabetes.
Thyroid numbers that fluctuate but are always described as “manageable.”
Cholesterol that no one brings up unless the report forces the conversation.

Seven pills a day.
Regular blood work.
And the same sentence every time I ask how he’s really doing — “I’m fine, don’t overthink so much.”

I tried everything a well-meaning, informed daughter would do.
Reminding him to walk.
Correcting food choices.
Forwarding articles.
Explaining why sugar spikes matter even when medicines are on board.

He listened.
Nodded.
And went back to the same chair, the same television, the same rhythm that slowly brought him here.

For a long time, I thought he was being stubborn.
Until I realised something uncomfortable.

His generation was never taught how to care for themselves — only how to carry responsibility quietly, ignore discomfort, and keep going no matter
what the body was asking for.

So I stopped trying to fix him.
And started changing the space around him.
Dinner moved slightly earlier, without calling it “healthy.”
One bowl of curd or dal became non-negotiable, without explaining protein.
Evening walks stopped being about steps and became about time together.
The phone went away at night, the TV stayed — sleep came easier.
 And I followed the same routines, so it never felt like instructions.
No strict diet.
No gym talk.
No fear-based warnings about the future.

Slowly, the sugar readings steadied.
BP became less erratic.
Digestion improved.
Sleep deepened.

But the biggest change wasn’t on paper.
It was in him.
Less irritability.
Less withdrawal.
More presence.

I learned this the hard way:
Indian parents don’t resist care.
They resist being treated like problems that need fixing.

I used to roll my eyes at GLP-1 drugs — Ozempic, Mounjaro, Wegovy.

Celebrities. Influencers. Even a few people I personally know were suddenly on them.
 My first reaction was skepticism:
 Doctors are prescribing this? Really?

Before joining the “it’s poison” chorus (which is common in the health space), I chose a different path.
 I decided to understand it properly.

So I did.
 Courses from reputed institutions.
 Clinical trials. Mechanisms of action. Side effects. Long-term data.
 And most importantly — real-world outcomes.

What I learned surprised me ⬇️

GLP-1 agonists are not inherently “bad.”
 They are powerful metabolic tools — especially for people with severe obesity and insulin resistance who have genuinely tried everything.

Here’s the part most people don’t know 👇

When insulin stays chronically high, fat cells are biochemically “locked.”
 Hunger hormones remain elevated.
 Satiety signals misfire.
 The brain keeps sending “eat” signals even at adequate calories.

⚠️ In this state, discipline alone often fails.
 Not because someone lacks willpower —
 but because biology is actively resisting weight loss.

For some people, losing 4–8 kg in the first 2–3 months on a GLP-1 is the first real win they’ve had in years.

That early progress does something powerful ✨
 It breaks the “nothing ever works for me” loop.
 Motivation returns.
 Habits finally become easier to sustain.

Used correctly, the drug becomes a bridge — not a crutch — to lifestyle change.

Now, let me be very clear ⛔

I’m not saying everyone should take it.
 I’m not saying it’s risk-free.

GLP-1s can come with:
Nausea and GI issues
Muscle loss if protein and strength training are neglected
Potential thyroid concerns (still being studied)
And yes — weight regain if lifestyle doesn’t change

But I also won’t label it “evil” when it has helped thousands finally gain traction after decades of struggle.

So the real question isn’t:
 “Is GLP-1 good or bad?”

It’s this ⬇️
 Are we using it as a shortcut instead of a bridge?
 Are we pairing it with real nutrition, resistance training, sleep and stress management — or expecting an injection to do lifelong work?

That’s where I draw the line.

Medication can open the door 🚪
 But only lifestyle walks through it — and stays.

What do you think?
 Bridge or shortcut?

Have you (or someone close) used a GLP-1?
 What actually happened after the initial weight loss?

Real stories > loud opinions.
 No judgment here.

I walked away from a career most people would have killed for.

Corporate HR. Three preschool franchises. A health food startup.

From the outside, it looked like I had figured it out.

But inside, I was watching something that quietly broke my heart.

Women working harder than anyone I knew.
Juggling careers, children, households, relationships.
Doing *everything right* on paper.

And still exhausted. Still stuck. Still invisible.

I saw it everywhere.

The high-performing woman passed over because her "energy seemed off."
The mother dropping her kids at 7 am, running on chai and guilt.
The "wellness" products sold to women who were actually depleted — and nobody connecting the dots.

And then I saw it in the mirror.

Thyroid climbing. Hair falling. Weight that wouldn't move no matter how hard I tried.

That was the moment I stopped asking "what is wrong with me?"

And started asking *what is my body actually trying to tell me?"

That question changed everything.

I reversed my thyroid without medication. Lost the weight without starving. And at 40, as a mom of two boys, I stepped onto a bodybuilding stage.

Not to prove something to the world.

But for every woman who had been told she was the problem.

She never was.

The information was.

“I have quit sugar. I eat salad every day.”
As a hormone health coach, I hear this so many times.

And honestly?

All I want to do is hug that woman and say:
“I’m so sorry for what the fitness industry has done to you.”

Somewhere along the way, women were made to believe that being healthy means:
saying no to every dessert,
eating dry salads while the family eats real food,
feeling guilty after a banana,
surviving on coffee, cucumber, and willpower,and calling it discipline.

Then they come to me exhausted.
Hair falling.
Periods irregular.
Cravings out of control.
Energy gone by 3 PM.
Workouts feeling harder every week.

And they say:
“But I’m eating so clean.”
That sentence breaks my heart.

Because a salad is not a badge of honour if your body is undernourished.

Hormones do not care how “clean” your Instagram plate looks.

They care whether your body is getting:
✔️ enough protein
✔️ enough calories
✔️ healthy fats
✔️ carbohydrates for energy
✔️ micronutrients
✔️ sleep and recovery

Real hormone health is not built on fear of sugar.

It is built on a body that feels safe, nourished, and supported.

So if you’re a woman who has been trying to be “good” for years — skipping treats, eating salads, and still feeling tired and stuck — please hear this:

You do not need more punishment.
You need better nourishment.

And that is a completely different conversation. 💛

“The arm around my shoulder lasted 5 seconds… and I wanted to freeze time.”

We were just taking a casual picture.
He came and put his arm around my shoulder for maybe 5 seconds.
That’s it.

I smiled for the camera, but inside something shifted.

Because if you’re a mother of a teenage son, you know these moments become rare, unexpected gifts.

There was a time when he would:

sit in my lap without invitation,
hold my hand everywhere,
tell me every random thing that happened in his day,
and hug me just because he walked past me.

Now he is taller than me.

He has his own world, his own friends, his own thoughts.

Sometimes I have to ask twice to get a full sentence. 😄

And yet… in that
 one small moment, with his arm around my shoulder, I could still feel my little boy hiding inside this growing young man.

Nobody prepares you for this stage of motherhood.

You spend years wishing they would grow up.

Then one day they do.
And suddenly you realise you would give anything to hold on to these tiny flashes of childhood that still visit you for a few seconds at a time.

So today I’m not posting a perfect photo.
I’m posting a reminder to myself:

Don’t miss the 5-second moments while waiting for the big milestones. 💛
Because sometimes motherhood lives in a quick side hug, a half smile, and an arm around your shoulder that disappears before you’re ready to let it go.

💬 Moms of teenagers — what is the one small thing your child still does that melts your heart every single time?

“Romance is wonderful, but in your late 30s and 40s, partnership often looks like one person handling the children while the other finishes a work call.”

This is probably the most honest thing I can say about marriage at this stage of life.

When we were younger, I thought a good relationship looked like:
long conversations,
spontaneous outings,
surprise plans,
endless time together.

Now?

A good day sometimes looks like:
he handles dinner while I finish client check-ins,
I manage the kids’ schedule while he takes an important call,
one of us is exhausted, so the other quietly picks up the slack,
we sit in the same room doing completely different things and still feel like we’re on the same side.

Somewhere between raising children, building careers, paying bills, supporting families, managing hormones, and trying not to lose ourselves, we stopped trying to be a perfect couple.

And honestly?

That has been one of the healthiest shifts in our marriage.
Because real relationships in your late 30s and 40s are rarely Instagram-perfect.

They are built in the ordinary moments:
the shared mental load,
the silent understanding,
the “I’ve got this, you rest,”
the coffee left on the table when the other person is rushing,
the patience on days when neither of you has much left to give.

As women, we often carry so many invisible tabs open in our minds:
school messages,
groceries,
work deadlines,
parents,
children,
our own health,
our own dreams.

And if we’re not careful, we start measuring our relationship by how romantic it looks instead of how supported we feel.

What I’ve learned is this:
Love after 15+ years is less about butterflies and more about bandwidth.

It’s about asking:
Are we still respecting each other?
Are we still making space for each other’s growth?
Are we still choosing “us” even when life is loud, messy, and exhausting?
There are days when my husband and I are not at our most romantic.

But if one of us is struggling, the other steps in.
And at this stage of life, that kind of partnership feels incredibly attractive.
So to every woman in her late 30s or 40s who worries that her marriage has become too practical, let me tell you something:

Practical is not the opposite of love.

Sometimes practical is what love looks like when two adults are building a life, raising children, chasing dreams, and still deciding—every single day—to be on the same team. ❤️

posts.text:
What I changed when my son wasn't eating enough.
In Part 1, I told you how worried I used to be when my younger one barely ate.

The biggest change wasn't forcing him to eat more.
It was making the food he DID eat more nutritious.

For a 5–8-year-old, I want parents to think about nutrient density, variety and consistency, not calorie counting.

Here are the things I started prioritising:
1. Protein at every main meal
Eggs, chicken, fish, paneer, curd, milk, dal, beans, soy/tofu — depending on what the child eats.

Not because children need a “high-protein diet.”
Because protein is one of the building blocks needed for growth and development.

2. Healthy fats
Nuts/nut butters, seeds, dairy, eggs, avocado, and appropriate cooking oils.
Especially for children who eat small portions, adding nutrient-dense foods can make those portions count.

3. Fruits AND vegetables
Not because vegetables are magically superior to everything else.

But because variety gives children different vitamins, minerals, fibre and other beneficial compounds.

And yes — if my child eats a banana happily, I'm not going to turn it into a negotiation about broccoli.

4. Carbohydrates are not the enemy.
Rice, roti, oats, potatoes, dosa, idli, bread, fruits and other grains can absolutely be part of a child's diet.

Children are growing and active.
They need energy.

5. I stopped making supplements the solution to everything.
A multivitamin is not a replacement for food.

Iron, vitamin D, B12 or other supplements may be appropriate when there is a deficiency, increased need, restricted diet or a healthcare professional recommends them.

Don't create a supplement stack for a healthy child just because Instagram told you they need one.

6. And perhaps most importantly — I stopped forcing food.
I offered nutritious food.
I created a routine.
I gave him choices within reasonable boundaries.

And I let him decide how much to eat.
My job was to decide what, when and where food was offered.
His job was to decide whether and how much he ate.

That shift reduced the anxiety around food for both of us.
And here's something I wish more mothers heard:

A child who eats less at one meal isn't necessarily a child who is undernourished.

Look at the bigger picture:
Growth.
Energy.
Development.
Activity.
Sleep.
Bowel habits.
Dietary variety.
And the pattern over time.

And if something genuinely concerns you — poor growth, persistent fatigue, very restricted eating, gastrointestinal symptoms or other changes — don't guess.
Get the child assessed.

My younger one's eating taught me something I now carry into my coaching:
Sometimes the solution isn't getting your child to eat MORE.

It's making the food you offer better, calmer and more nutrient-dense.

And sometimes…
the best thing you can take off a child's plate is the pressure.

They won't remember whether I missed a workout.
They won't remember whether my jeans were one size smaller.

But they may remember something else.

Whether their mother was always worried about her body.
Whether she refused dessert because she was “being good.”
Whether she looked in the mirror and criticised herself.
Whether she spent every holiday thinking about what she had eaten.

Or whether she simply lived. ❤️
This has changed the way I think about health.

I still care about nutrition.
I care deeply about strength.
I care about blood work.
I care about metabolic health.
I care about taking care of my body.

But I don't want my children to grow up believing that health means constantly trying to become smaller.

I want them to see me:
🏋️‍♀️ Lift weights.
🥗 Eat nourishing food.
🍰 Enjoy a birthday cake without guilt.
✈️ Travel and experience life.
😴 Rest when I'm tired.
❤️ Take care of my health.

And still live my life.
Because one day, they're going to have bodies of their own.
And I don't want to hand them my insecurities.

I want to hand them knowledge.
I want them to know how to nourish themselves.

How to build strength.
How to understand their health markers.
How to recognise when something feels wrong.

And most importantly:
How to live in their body without spending their entire life fighting it.
Maybe that's one of the greatest responsibilities we have as parents.
Not teaching our children to have perfect bodies.
Teaching them not to hate the bodies they have.

And perhaps the example we set every day teaches them far more than the things we say.

Our children are watching how we treat ourselves.

𝐈 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐚 𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐡 𝐜𝐨𝐚𝐜𝐡 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐈 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐩𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬.

I actually came to this work through three completely different businesses.
First, I ran preschools.
Then I built a health-food startup.
And eventually, I became a hormonal health coach.

For a long time, even I thought my career looked scattered.
𝐈𝐭 𝐰𝐚𝐬𝐧'𝐭.

There was one lesson running through all three.
People don't fail because they don't know what to do.
They fail when the system around them makes the right thing difficult to do.

I saw it with children.
You can tell a child to behave differently all day.
Or you can change the environment, the routine and the cues around them.

I saw it again with food.
You can tell someone to eat healthy.

But if healthy food is inconvenient, expensive, boring or impossible to fit into their schedule, information isn't going to win.

Then I started coaching women.
And suddenly I was seeing the same thing at a much deeper level.

Women already knew they should:
🥚 Eat protein.
🏋️‍♀️ Exercise.
😴 Sleep.
🍬 Reduce sugar.
🚶‍♀️ Move more.
🧘‍♀️ Manage stress.

They weren't short of information.
They were trying to apply generic advice to very specific bodies and very complicated lives.

A woman in her 40s with perimenopause doesn't necessarily need the same strategy that worked at 28.

A woman with hypothyroidism doesn't need to be told simply to "eat less."

A woman with insulin resistance doesn't need another punishment-based diet.

And a woman who has been dieting for 15 years doesn't necessarily need more discipline.

She needs better diagnosis of the problem.
That's probably the biggest shift I've made as a coach.

I stopped asking:
“What plan should I give her?”

And started asking:
👉 “What is actually preventing this plan from working?”

That's the difference between giving advice and coaching.
And perhaps that's what all my previous careers were teaching me without my realising it.

Systems beat willpower.
 Root causes beat quick fixes.

Your turn:
What is one piece of health advice you've followed for years that simply stopped working for you?

I'd genuinely love to know. 👇

𝐁𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐦𝐢𝐬𝐬 𝐚 𝐬𝐲𝐦𝐩𝐭𝐨𝐦 𝐚𝐬 “𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬,” 𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐬𝐞 𝟓 𝐩𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐬. 🔎

This is the checklist I wish more women knew.
Because the interesting information isn't always what you're experiencing.

Sometimes it's when it happens.

1️⃣ Does it happen at the same time every day?
4 PM exhaustion is different from random fatigue.
3 AM waking is different from simply sleeping badly.
The timing itself can be information.

2️⃣ Does it follow your menstrual cycle? 🔄
Energy.
Hunger.
Sleep.
Cravings.
Mood.
Training performance.
If the same thing appears at roughly the same phase every month, that's a pattern worth recording.

3️⃣ Does it appear BEFORE your bloodwork changes? 🧪
This is one of the most interesting things I've seen with clients.
Sometimes a woman says:
“I knew something was off before I got the report.”
Don't treat that feeling as a diagnosis.
But don't dismiss it either.
Write it down.
Then see whether the pattern repeats.

4️⃣ Did the symptom begin AFTER something changed? ⚠️
New medication?
Diet?
Training volume?
Sleep?
Stress?
Weight change?
A symptom appearing after a change gives you a much better starting point than simply saying:
“I've always been tired.”

5️⃣ What happens when the symptom IMPROVES? 👀
This is the question almost nobody asks.
If your energy improves, what else changed?
If your sleep improves, what else changed?
If your cravings disappear, what else changed?
You are looking for relationships, not magic explanations.

Here's the rule I'd save:
**One symptom = a complaint.
A recurring pattern = information.
 A verified pattern = something worth investigating.**
And this is why I want women to become better observers of their own bodies.
Not to diagnose themselves.
Not to Google every symptom.
Not to become anxious about every fluctuation.

To become better at noticing.

Because by the time something shows up dramatically on a report, your body may have been whispering about it for months.

📌 Save this for your next health check-up.

And tell me:
Which symptom in your body has a very specific pattern that you've never been able to explain? 👇

“Your TSH is normal. So your thyroid is fine.”
I wish thyroid health were that simple.
Because one of the most misunderstood things about thyroid testing is this:

TSH is not made by your thyroid.
It is made by your pituitary gland.
Think of it as a message.
Your brain–pituitary system is essentially telling your thyroid:

“We need more thyroid hormone.”
Your thyroid then responds by producing thyroid hormones — primarily T4, which can be converted into the more active T3.
And this is where things get interesting.
Because when you look at your blood report and see:

TSH — NORMAL ✅
that doesn't mean you've measured everything that matters about thyroid function.
You're looking at one part of the communication system.
Not the entire story.
And this matters because I've seen women come in saying:

“My reports are normal. But I don't feel normal.”
They're exhausted.
They're struggling with weight.
Their hair has changed.
They're cold when everyone else is comfortable.
Their periods have changed.
Their mood and energy aren't what they used to be.
And they've been told:

“Your TSH is fine. It's probably stress.”
Now, to be clear — symptoms like these aren't proof that your thyroid is the cause.
But they deserve context.
Your symptoms, TSH, free T4, medications, other health conditions and the bigger clinical picture all matter.
Because your thyroid isn't an isolated organ.
It's part of an entire regulatory system.

So the next time someone tells you:
“Your thyroid is normal because your TSH is normal.”
pause.

Ask:
“What exactly did we test — and what are we actually trying to understand?”

Because good thyroid care isn't about chasing one perfect number.
It's about understanding the woman behind the report.
Save this for the next time you get told, “Everything is normal.” 🫶

She lost 3.6 kg in six months.
And honestly?
I was thrilled.

Not because 3.6 kg is some extraordinary number.
But because I knew what it had taken to get there.
She had spent years doing what most women are told to do when their weight doesn't cooperate:
Eat less.
Exercise more.
Try harder.
Start again.
Lose some weight.
Gain it back.
Feel like she'd failed.
And then punish herself a little harder the next time.

So when she came to me, losing weight quickly wasn't actually the hardest part.

The harder part was getting her body — and her relationship with food — out of that constant lose → regain → restrict → repeat cycle.

We weren't chasing a dramatic 30-day transformation.
We were looking at what was happening underneath the weight.
Her insulin resistance.
Her energy.
Her habits.
Her ability to stay consistent without feeling like she was constantly “on a diet.”

And most importantly —

we weren't building another plan she'd eventually have to recover from.
This is something I wish more women understood.
Because the fitness industry has made us believe that the faster you lose, the better the result.

But what if you lose 7 kg...
and regain 10?
And what if someone else loses 3.6 kg...
and doesn't regain it?
Which woman actually got the better result?
That's the part we don't talk about enough.

Weight loss isn't the only outcome I'm watching.
I'm watching whether your energy improves.
Whether your blood markers improve.
Whether your hunger becomes manageable.
Whether you can eat like a normal human being again.
Whether you can have a stressful week without completely falling off.
Whether the habits still exist six months later.

Because sometimes...
slow isn't a sign that the plan isn't working.
Sometimes, slow is what happens when we're finally building something that can last.
I wrote her full story in this week's The Health Edit.
And if you've spent years believing that your body only responds when you punish it harder...

I snapped at my son over a wet towel on the bed.

It wasn't about the towel.

As the mother of a teenager, I know the eye-roll, the closed door, the "Mumma, chill."

And honestly?
Some days my patience runs out faster than his.

For a long time I thought that made me a worse mother.

Then I started looking at it as a hormone health coach.

In your late 30s and 40s, progesterone often starts dropping first, sometimes years before your periods change.
Progesterone is your calming hormone.
When it dips, many women notice:
a shorter fuse,
lighter sleep,
anxiety that comes out of nowhere,
crying at an ad and then feeling silly about it.

Now add a teenager who is learning to be his own person.
Two bodies going through big hormonal shifts under one roof. 😄

That is not bad parenting.
That is biology meeting real life.

What helps me:
- protecting my sleep like it's a client appointment
- protein at breakfast, so I'm not running on chai and fumes
- strength training 4 days a week, my best stress outlet
- saying "I need 5 minutes" before I say something I regret

He still rolls his eyes.
But every now and then, he still puts his arm around me without being asked.
I'll take it. 

Moms of teenagers, what tests your patience the most right now?

𝐇𝐞 𝐓𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐄𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲𝐨𝐧𝐞. 𝐖𝐡𝐨 𝐓𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐇𝐢𝐦?

He pays the EMIs. 
He drives his parents to every appointment. 
He's the first to show up when anyone needs anything.

When did anyone last ask how he's doing?

I coach women. But I see the men in the background of their stories.

The husband awake at 2 AM doing the maths on school fees, the home loan and his fathers medical bills. Who says Im fine the next morning and goes back to work.

Nobody taught him a different sentence.

Boys learn early: don't cry, handle it, be the strong one. By 40, he's an expert at carrying and a beginner at asking. 

His body keeps the account. 

Chronic stress keeps cortisol up and sleep short. In one well-known study, healthy young men who slept five hours a night for a week had 10-15% lower daytime testosterone. Add rising blood pressure, belly fat and blood sugar. South Asian men also tend to develop heart disease years earlier than men elsewhere. 

And he won't tell you. Many men see a doctor only after something is already broken.   

𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐚𝐬 𝐬𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝. 

Here's the part I find most striking.

The woman who is everyones emergency contact is very often married to the man who is everyones silent provider. Two exhausted people in one house, each quietly assuming the other has it easier.

If you love a man like this, three small things: 

1. Ask How are you actually doing? Then ask it a second time. The first answer is always fine.
2. Book the annual check-up he keeps postponing: blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids, vitamin D, B12, thyroid.
3. Protect his sleep like a medical treatment. It is one. 

𝘐𝘧 𝘺𝘰𝘶'𝘳𝘦 𝘢 𝘸𝘰𝘮𝘢𝘯 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴, 𝘴𝘦𝘯𝘥 𝘪𝘵 𝘵𝘰 him.If 𝘺𝘰𝘶'𝘳𝘦 𝘩𝘪𝘮, 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘴𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘳 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘮𝘪𝘴𝘴𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘴𝘭𝘪𝘱.

𝐍𝐚𝐯𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐫𝐢 𝐭𝐨 𝐃𝐢𝐰𝐚𝐥𝐢: 𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐭𝐨 𝐄𝐚𝐭, 𝐒𝐥𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐇𝐲𝐝𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐢𝐧 𝐍𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫

𝘐𝘍𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘷𝘦 𝘴𝘦𝘢𝘴𝘰𝘯 𝘪𝘴𝘯'𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮.
𝘈𝘭𝘭-𝘰𝘳-𝘯𝘰𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘪𝘴.
"𝘐'𝘭𝘭 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘳𝘵 𝘢𝘨𝘢𝘪𝘯 𝘢𝘧𝘵𝘦𝘳 𝘋𝘪𝘸𝘢𝘭𝘪" 𝘪𝘴 𝘩𝘰𝘸 𝘮𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘸𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘯 𝘭𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘴𝘪𝘹 𝘸𝘦𝘦𝘬𝘴.

Between now and the end of the festive season, you'll have fasts, feasts, late nights and sweets in every kitchen. You don't need a strict plan. You need three anchors.

𝟏. 𝐄𝐀𝐓𝐈𝐍𝐆

Don't save up for the feast. Skipping breakfast and lunch to "make room" sends blood sugar on a rollercoaster, and by evening your body is begging for sugar.

Eat protein and vegetables first, sweets after, never on an empty stomach. Protein and fibre before carbohydrate lowers the glucose spike.

Fasting days: sabudana, potato and kuttu are mostly starch. Pair them with paneer, curd, makhana or nuts so you don't crash by 4 PM. Break the fast with protein, not only sweets.

Walk 10–15 minutes after the big meal. It is the simplest tool we have for lowering the post-meal glucose rise.

𝟐. 𝐒𝐋𝐄𝐄𝐏

One short night raises hunger and cravings the next day. Late nights are coming, so protect one thing: your wake-up time, within an hour of normal.

Make up the sleep the next night; don't cover it with caffeine all day.

Alcohol and heavy meals close to bedtime fragment sleep. Eat dinner earlier on the nights you can.

𝟑. 𝐇𝐘𝐃𝐑𝐀𝐓𝐈𝐎𝐍

Festive food is salty, sweet and fried, and you'll be sweating in the kitchen. Start the day with water before chai, keep a bottle where you can see it, and add electrolytes (a pinch of salt and lemon, or ORS) on fasting days and heavy-sweat days.

The day after: don't punish. No fasting, no extra workout. The next meal is a normal meal. One day of mithai doesn't undo months. The reset mindset does.

On thyroid medication? Take it on an empty stomach, and keep calcium, iron and heavy dairy sweets about 4 hours away from it.

For two years, she did everything “right.”
Iron tablets. A haematologist. Regular blood tests.

📍 Ferritin — March 2024: 5.18
📍 Ferritin — July 2026: 6.30

Two years of effort, and it moved by about one point.
When she came to me, her haemoglobin was 9.8.
She was tired, her hair was falling, and she had quietly accepted that her body was “just like this.”
Nobody had asked her one question:

Is the iron actually getting in?

Here's something important to understand:
Swallowing iron doesn't mean you absorb it.
Your gut has to take it in, and your daily routine can quietly interfere with that process.
So we didn't start by adding more iron.

We looked at what was getting in the way.

Here's what we addressed. 👇
🔎 1. GUT FIRST
We addressed her gut health and completed a deworming course before expecting absorption to improve.
⏰ 2. TIMING MATTERS
She was taking iron one hour after her thyroid tablet.
The two interfere with each other, and the usual advice is to keep them at least 4 hours apart.
She discovered this herself, and we moved her iron to dinner.
🔄 3. EVERY OTHER DAY
Studies show that alternate-day iron dosing can improve absorption in some circumstances.

Why?

A daily dose increases a hormone called hepcidin, which can temporarily reduce iron absorption from the next dose.

🥗 4. THE RIGHT FOOD RULES
We separated iron from tea, coffee and calcium, but not from all food.
She had been skipping meals around her iron supplementation and crashing as a result.
And then came the follow-up report.

✨ Nine weeks later, her ferritin was 34.62.
Look at the difference:
📊 Two years: +1
📊 Nine weeks: +28

When I shared the report, she barely reacted.
After two years of disappointment, I understood why.
One good number doesn't undo years of being let down.
She's not "done" yet.
We're aiming for 70+.
The same retest also showed that her thyroid needed attention, so she went back to her endocrinologist, who adjusted her dose.
And that's how it should work.
Coach and doctor. Each doing their part.
But the lesson stands.
If you've been on iron for months and your numbers won't move, the answer is rarely just "take more."
Ask what’s stopping it from getting in.
👇 If this sounds like your reports, comment "IRON" and I'll tell you what to check first.
